advancedsteelmaking-text:
Steelmaking Expanded adds a full industrial pipeline for turning out iron and steel in bulk, and it works in two stages. In Stage I you build a Blast Furnace and the support machinery around it to smelt iron, and in Stage II you bolt a Bessemer Converter onto that line to refine the molten iron into steel. Build the iron stage first and get it running reliably, because the steel stage is expensive and feeds directly from it. Be warned that the blast furnace is built from tier-3 refractory bricks, so you must already have reached the steel age to attempt it, and none of this machinery runs without steam power - have a steam setup working before you start.

The full chain is spread across four companion articles. The Blast Furnace is the heart of the operation and where Stage I begins; Hot Blast & Gas Handling covers the cowper stoves, the smoke stack and how everything ties into the pipe network, without which the furnace will never reach iron's melting point; Molten Metal & Casting explains the canals, taps and molds that turn the melt into finished items and where to route surplus metal or waste slag; and The Bessemer Converter opens Stage II, the heavy machinery that blows iron into steel and draws on every mechanic before it. The pipes, boilers and engines that power all of this come from the companion mod - see Steam Power - and are used both to supply mechanical power and to pressurise the air the furnace breathes. The furnace itself is an Ironworking Expanded shaft furnace at heart: the burden, the charge piles and the molten canals all come from that mod, and its Ironworking articles cover them in depth.

In brief, a full iron run goes like this. You prepare burden - crushed iron ore fluxed with lime - at an Ironworking Expanded Burdenmaker, and bake coke from coal in a coke oven. The furnace takes the two as alternating layers, nothing premixed: you load the Reinforced Hopper with coke and let the Bell Hopper beneath it lay the layer down the shaft, then load burden, and so on in rounds until the shaft is full. Lay coke first, because the furnace lights itself the moment an unbroken course of fuel covers the bottom of the shaft - there is no door and no torch. A powered Air Blower on a steam engine pushes air through a heated Cowper Stove and in through the Tuyeres as hot pressurised blast, while the Smoke Stack vents the excess gases. You hold the furnace past iron's melting point of about 1482 °C in the melting phase, alternating between two cowper stoves so the incoming air never goes cold, and once iron and slag have pooled you open the Molten Metal Taps to drain them down the canals into molds or barrels before they have a chance to solidify. Keep the rounds coming, the exhaust flowing and the boilers boiling, and repeat.
handbook-blastfurnace-text:
The Blast Furnace is the heart of the whole operation: a tall multiblock built mostly from refractory brick, with two tuyeres (blast intakes) low on the shaft, two gas outlets high up and a sealed top crowned by its two hoppers. Place the Blast Furnace Core first - it is the control block, sitting at the bottom centre of the hearth floor - then hold ctrl + shift + rightmouse on it to see the build outline and fill in every highlighted block until the structure reports itself complete. All told it needs 99 tier-3 refractory bricks - exactly tier 3, no lesser brick will do - plus the core, two tuyeres, an Iron Tap low in one wall with a Slag Tap one course higher in the opposite wall, two Pipe Outlets for the exhaust, a Reinforced Hopper and a Bell Hopper. The hollow shaft inside is left empty - that is where the charge goes. Mind the facings on the taps and tuyeres: a part fitted the wrong way round will not complete the structure, so turn it until the outline accepts it.

The furnace does not eat ore. It eats burden - crushed iron ore fluxed with lime, made at an Ironworking Expanded Burdenmaker - and it eats coke, and the two go in as separate, alternating layers; nothing is premixed. The Reinforced Hopper on top is the loading tank, and it holds one material at a time on purpose: one load lays one layer. rightmouse with charge in hand adds one unit, ctrl + rightmouse adds the whole stack, and an empty hand draws the tank back out. The Bell Hopper below pulls from the tank and drips the charge down the shaft, always into the lowest column, so the layers lie level on their own; dropping is on by default, an empty-handed ctrl + rightmouse on the hopper toggles it, and it stops by itself once the shaft is full. So you charge in rounds: fill the tank with coke and let it drain, then with burden, then coke again. Coke is baked from coal in a coke oven - raw coal is no fuel here at all - and charcoal is accepted at half the carbon, so a shaft charged with it runs cooler. Crush your ore in a pulverizer; even scrap iron bits crush back into crushed iron and go round again.

There is no door and no torch. The furnace lights itself the moment a complete course of fuel stands at the bottom of the shaft, in front of the tuyeres - which is why coke goes down first. Burden on its own cannot burn, and coke can never be slipped in beneath burden that is already laid, so a charge started with burden will never catch; if that happens, take the charge back out (an empty-handed rightmouse on a charge pile in the shaft takes a band off the top, and breaking a pile drops its contents) and start over with fuel. Once lit, the fire lives in front of the tuyeres, and the coke burns whether or not iron is being made - a lit furnace left standing is spending its charge on nothing.

To melt, the fire needs air and heat. The tuyeres drink pressurised air off the pipe network, and how much pressure the charge demands depends on how it was laid - a coke-lean charge packs dense and must be blown much harder. On plain cold air a standard charge stalls short of iron's melting line of about 1482 °C; hot blast is what carries it past. Charge a Cowper Stove on the furnace's own exhaust and route the blast through it - the Hot Blast article covers that half of the plant - and the furnace enters the melting phase, rendering the burden into molten pig iron and slag. Point at the core while it runs: block-info shows what the furnace is doing, the temperature against the threshold it must clear, both sides of the heat ledger and the grade of the burden, so a stall reads as a number and not a mystery. One stall deserves its own name: an under-fuelled charge arrives at the tuyeres too cold to melt and hangs - the furnace stays lit and hot, keeps eating its coke, and simply stops making iron. The core reports the hang; break the cold piles out of the bottom and charge richer.

Molten pig iron pools behind the lower tap and slag behind the upper one, and each tap needs the start of a molten canal beneath its spout before an empty-handed rightmouse will toggle the pour. Keep the taps open while it melts: the pools have a ceiling, and anything rendered over a full pool is lost. The fire itself ends a few ways. It goes out when the fuel at the tuyeres runs out - a campaign lasts exactly as long as the coke you laid - and it smothers if the exhaust backs up, so keep the outlets flowing through the cowpers and the smoke stack. Losing the blast does not kill it; the furnace falls back to a cool natural-draught burn, too cold to melt, until the air returns. Breaking a wall lets it burn on through the hole, but a breached furnace can never relight until it is repaired. And when it does go out, whatever was still molten freezes onto the hearth floor as solidified pig to be mined back out, while the unburnt charge stays standing in the shaft - dig it out through the piles, and expect what is left to be richer in coke toward the top.
handbook-hotblast-text:
Hot blast is preheated, pressurised air, and it is what lets the furnace climb hot enough to actually melt iron. A bare blast furnace tops out around 1400 °C, short of iron's melting point; to push past that you reclaim the heat the furnace throws away in its exhaust and feed it back in through the air. For this to work the air you supply must be both pressurised above about 2.5 atm and heated above roughly 800 °C.

Everything breathes through pipes from Low Pressure Expanded, and here a network carries one of two gases: ordinary air, and the hot exhaust that spills from the furnace. A handful of machines move it around. The Air Blower is a steam-engine sub-machine that pressurises air and forces it through the cowper stoves and into the furnace tuyeres. Valves open and close a line by hand, which you will need constantly for swapping the cowper stoves over and steering flow through the network, while pressure valves open by themselves above their gate pressure to spill overflow to another side (their input side wears a copper-textured rim). Outlets connect a network to a structure's face and form part of its multiblock footprint. Each network tracks its gas type, volume and temperature, and any open-ended pipe leaks, so plan how many machines you run carefully to avoid under- or over-supplying.

The Cowper Stove is a heat regenerator, and it is what makes the air hot. Pipe the furnace's exhaust into a stove and it soaks that heat into the heatsink at its core - "charging" - which you can speed up by burning a coal pile inside, fastest of all with anthracite; just beware that burning low grades of coal makes the stove itself give off exhaust from its main output. Once charged, route plain pressurised air through the same stove and it pours out scorching hot, and fed into the tuyeres it drives the furnace's internal temperature back up toward about 1700 °C. Each stove needs 48 refractory bricks of any tier, a cowper stove intake as its control block, four heat sinks, two pipe outlets, one straight pipe passthrough and an iron hatch door, with one slot below the intake left open for the coal pile that speeds the exchange.

A single stove can only do one job at a time, and a charged core runs down as you draw heat from it, so you run two stoves as a pair: while one charges on exhaust, the other discharges hot air to the furnace, and when the discharging one drops below 800 °C you swap their roles with valves. Keep exhaust and air on separate paths, because if they mix inside a stove it cannot heat up.

A blast furnace also makes more exhaust than the stoves can swallow, and a backed-up exhaust line will choke and extinguish it, so the Smoke Stack vents the surplus to the sky and acts as the safety valve of the whole system. It needs a smoke stack intake as its control block, 24 refractory bricks of any tier and 36 of any ordinary brick. Above all, keep an eye on the stoves' temperature - let them cool and the furnace will stop smelting or go out entirely.
handbook-casting-text:
Molten metal is plumbed, not carried. You lay a Molten Canal (Start) as the anchor of a network and run straights, bends and junctions out from it, all crafted from cobblestone (or burned brick for a tidier look) and fire clay. The furnace is drained through its Molten Metal Taps - the lower tap pours iron and the upper one pours slag - and each tap needs the start of a canal beneath it before it will let you toggle it with rightmouse. At the far end a Canal Tap pours into a barrel, useful when you have excess to drain; bear in mind that molten iron actually flows through the canals as a simulation, so not everything will necessarily drain.

An empty straight canal can be sealed by hand to act as a manual valve: rightmouse it with four fire clay and it caps over, severing the network at that block, and a chisel reopens it and recovers two of the clay. Only a drained canal can be sealed, but it is a handy way to choose which path the metal takes when several are open to it.

Watch the temperature throughout, because metal in the canals cools slowly and will solidify in place if it drops too far. A hardened canal stops flowing and must be chipped clear; once it has cooled enough, a chisel and hammer recover most of the metal as bits, which can themselves be crushed back into crushed iron for the furnace. Keep your runs short, keep them fed, and empty them before they - or the furnace - go cold.

Casting itself happens at two kinds of destination. A Mold Pedestal casts small tool molds: shift + rightmouse places or removes the mold and ctrl + rightmouse toggles the pour. The big anvil and helve-hammer molds go directly under the canal tap instead. The other destination is a Molten Barrel, bulk storage for liquid metal that you can use to buffer excess iron or to hold slag from the top tap; when its contents solidify you can chisel them out just like a canal, as long as you set the barrel on the ground first.

Freshly filled molds are dangerously hot, and carrying one bare-handed will burn you, so wear heavy leather or a blacksmith's gloves. While the metal is still liquid the mold can only ride in your empty active hand - stashing it in a bag or on a rack spills the metal at once - so set it down, let it harden, and then collect the casting with a plain rightmouse.

Finally, slag is not just waste. Solidified slag grinds into powdered slag, which mixed with slaked lime in a barrel yields mortar, and spread over farmland acts as a phosphate fertilizer - a furnace byproduct turned into building stock and crop yield.
handbook-bessemer-text:
The Bessemer process is how you turn raw iron into steel. Raw iron carries too much contamination - excess carbon, sulfur and other elements - and the idea is to literally boil the iron by blowing air through it, burning those impurities out and purifying it into mild steel. The Bessemer Converter is the machine that does it, taking molten iron and blowing it into steel. It is the most demanding machine in the mod - it draws both mechanical power and a supply of pressurised air, and only works as the final stage of an already-running molten line - so do not attempt it until your iron tier is well established.

The converter is a 3x3x3 vessel raised through right-click construction. Place its control block first, then rightmouse it with one large gear and eight iron or steel rods in your hotbar to start the vessel, and build it up through its stages until it reports complete. Around the vessel sit its service ports - a gas intake, a mechanical transmission, an input tap, and an output canal-start block. Beyond the control block itself you will need the converter (raised in place from the gear and rods), a Bessemer transmission, a Bessemer gas intake, and a short run of molten canal: one start, two straights and a tap. The vessel's own construction stages consume, all together, 40 iron or steel plates, 42 nails-and-strips, 18 rods, 84 tier-3 refractory bricks, 84 fire clay and three straight gas pipes.

Powering it draws on two services from the systems you have already built. For mechanical power, connect an axle to the transmission so the vessel can tilt and blow - a steam engine is recommended here for the torque it needs. For air, pipe pressurised air from a blower into the converter's gas intake, which must face the same way as the control block or it will not couple. Then run a molten canal from a furnace tap into the converter's input tap, and a second canal beneath it will carry the finished output toward your molds.

To operate it, set the converter to Filling and pour molten iron in from the canal until it holds as much as you want (it need not be full to run). Switch it to Normal, and with power and air both flowing it refines the charge at about 1800 °C for roughly five minutes into steel. Finally set it to Pouring to drain the finished steel into the output canal, from where it travels the molten network exactly like iron.

The same temperature rule applies inside the vessel: if the charge cools and solidifies before you pour it, you must break the converter with a steel pickaxe to recover the metal and then rebuild, so make sure you can drain it in time. One last note - a single blast furnace produces more iron than one converter can consume, so you will want at least two converters running for continuous steel. All of this machinery takes a great deal of space both horizontally and vertically, and you should make sure every valve and control is easy to reach, because time spent struggling to get at something is time your metal spends solidifying or your furnace spends cooling. This may finally be the moment you build the factory you always wanted.

handbook-highpressure-text:
High Pressure Expanded adds the top of the steam chain: a bigger boiler that raises steam into the high band, and an engine efficient enough to spend it well. Both are steel builds and both assume the low-pressure loop already works - read Steam Power: Boilers and Steam Power: Engines first, because everything there about construction stages, priming, sub-machines and repairs applies here unchanged. The fire is the one thing that does not: the Cornish carries its grate inside its own shell, while this boiler burns a coal pile you lay and light yourself.

The larger Lancashire Boiler is a twin-flue design that delivers higher pressures and greater volumes for the more demanding machines, though be ready for the steel it costs. It takes 36 steel plates, 24 nails-and-strips and 12 rods with 64 fire bricks. Once the stages are done there is nothing to build around it: set a coal pile alight in the open cell at its firing end and keep it fed, and run your steam pipe up from the port on top. The brickwork in the model is part of the model - the game asks for none of it. It reaches up to 48 L/s and 12 atm, with a 1200 L vessel that needs 200 L to begin boiling.

The Cornish Engine is the more advanced design, working at higher pressure and wringing the same power from less steam because it can regulate how much steam enters the cylinder. Running at 6-8 atm, its control rod sets a working rate of Low, Normal or High that draws 8, 16 or 32 L/s of steam and delivers 0.2, 0.4 or 0.8 units of power respectively (an internal value); on High it will comfortably drive six helve hammers, and that same setting also scales how much water an attached pump moves. Its construction stages cost the same materials as the Watt engine - the difference in price lies in the engine's main block.

The two are built for each other, but not blindly: the Lancashire's 12 atm ceiling sits well above the Cornish engine's 8 atm breaking point, so put a pressure valve between them, with an overflow pipe, exactly as you would between a Cornish boiler and a Watt engine. Throttling the engine up raises the pressure it needs to engage as well as the steam it drinks, so a line that runs a Low setting comfortably may sit below the High setting's engage pressure entirely.
blockdesc-pipe-*: High-pressure rolled steel piping. The strongest of the three pipe tiers.
